newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks seen bearish until August.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks seen bearish until August.

text.p: Hopes for an improvement in Thai stocks, beset by nagging economic ills, are fading and analysts now believe the market will not recover before August.
Some analysts had previously forecast that the Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index would break out of the doldrums by late March.

But concerns over Thailand's slowing economy, tight liquidity in the money market, rumours of a baht devaluation, and a slide in the value of the local currency continue to erode confidence and push investors to the sidelines.
The recent default of Thai property developer Somprasong Land Plc proved too much for the market to handle, driving the SET index to a four-and-a-half year low on Friday.
Analysts said they have been forced to postpone their recovery projections for the bourse and now think it will not start to pick up until the end of the first half.
After a dismal week, the composite SET index finished 1.38 points lower at 747.76 on Friday, the lowest close since August 31, 1992, when the index finished at 746.51.

"Investment in the stock market is expected to remain sluggish because of these negative factors until the end of the first half of this year," said Somchai Trairattanapirom, vice president of SITCA Investment and Securities.
"The index is expected to move between 700 and 850 points during the period."

The troubles at Somprasong have rippled through the market, raising fears over the stability of some Thai property companies and their creditors and introducing a fresh element of uncertainty which could hurt near-term sentiment, analysts said.
Somprasong became the first Thai firm to default on a Euroconvertible debenture interest payment last week when it failed to honour $3.1 million in debt due on its $80 million issue.
But analysts said investment in the stock market, especially by foreigners, could rebound following an improvement in the country's exports and its gaping current account deficit.
Thailand's current account deficit stood at 8.2 percent of gross domestic product in 1996.
A government panel, chaired by Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan, said last week that exports were targeted to grow 10 percent in 1997 to 1.56 trillion baht.
Tight liquidity and the weak baht have also hurt stocks.

"Tight liquidity prevailing in the market now due to demand for cash during the Chinese New Year and the weak baht against the dollar are big worries now," analyst Thanawat Patchimkul of Seamico Securities said.
The baht weakened to 25.990-26.040 against the U.S. dollar late on Friday from 25.985-25.995 late on Thursday following the dollar's strength abroad, dealers said.
Both Somchai and Thanawat agreed that investors would now prefer to invest in the foreign exchange market rather than stocks because it offered higher returns and less risk.
They said investors were awaiting for an outcome of a meeting of Group of Seven (G7) finance ministers and central bank heads in Berlin on Saturday.

"If the G7 agrees to support the dollar and find measures on not letting it to become too strong against the yen it would help the baht definitely. This may induce many investors to return to the stock market," Thanawat said.
The ministers signalled on Saturday that they would try to halt the rise in the U.S. dollar by indicating they wanted major exchange rates to stabilise around current levels.
They suggested at the G7 meeting that the dollar had climbed enough from its record lows of 1995 and called for currency stability to create the conditions for world economic growth.
